intro:
Older customers phone orders restaurant owners deal with every day often come down to one thing: make the call easy. Speak slowly, keep the menu simple, and confirm the order in plain language.

A lot of older regulars still prefer calling because it feels familiar. They may want to ask about the soup, parking, or whether their usual item is available. ROAL can help with that by answering the phone, taking orders from the live menu, and handing harder questions to staff with a summary.

sections.h2: Why do older regulars still call instead of ordering online?
sections.body:
Older regulars often call because they know the routine. They may not want to open an app, remember a password, or scroll through a long menu. They may also want a quick human-style answer about hours, parking, or whether the special is still on.

That means the phone is not just a backup. For many independent spots, it is a real sales channel. A simple phone experience matters more than fancy tech. Try to make the call feel like this:

"Thanks for calling Tony’s Deli. How can I help you today?"

Here is what older callers usually need from you:
- A clear greeting
- Slow, plain wording
- One question at a time
- A repeat-back of the order
- A ready time they can trust

If your team is busy, a phone host like ROAL can answer these routine questions and take the order without making the caller wait on hold.

sections.h2: What should the phone script sound like for older callers?
sections.body:
Keep the script short. Older callers often do better when you sound calm and direct. Do not rush through item names or modifiers. Say the price and ready time in a way that is easy to repeat back.

A simple script can look like this:

1. Greeting: "Thank you for calling."
2. Offer help: "Pickup or delivery?"
3. Take the order one item at a time.
4. Repeat the order back slowly.
5. Give the ready time.

Use language like:
- "Would you like regular or large?"
- "Do you want onions on that?"
- "I have one plain pepperoni and one chicken parm sandwich."
- "Your pickup will be ready around 20 minutes."

For callers who ask something unusual, it sends the question to staff with context so you do not have to start from zero.

sections.h2: How do you keep the order accurate without making the caller repeat everything?
sections.body:
Accuracy matters more with older regulars because they often order the same items every week. If you interrupt too much, they may lose track. If you move too fast, they may agree to the wrong thing. The goal is to confirm, not quiz them.

Use a simple check format like this:

| Step | What to confirm |
|---|---|
| Main item | Sandwich, pizza, dinner, or soup |
| Size | Small, medium, large, slice, platter |
| Modifiers | No onion, extra cheese, light sauce |
| Notes | Cut in half, sauce on the side, well done |
| Contact | Name and phone number |
| Timing | Ready time or delivery timing |

A good phone line is:

"Just to confirm, that is one turkey club, no tomato, with fries, and one plain slice. Is that right?"

sections.h2: How do you handle common questions from older customers?
sections.body:
Older callers often ask the same practical questions. That is normal. They want reassurance before they place the order. The best approach is to answer these clearly and in the same order every time.

Common questions to prepare for:
- What are your hours?
- Where are you located?
- Is there parking?
- What comes on the sandwich or platter?
- Is this item spicy or contains nuts or shellfish?

A usable response sounds like this:

"Yes, we are open until 9. We’re at 24 Main Street, and there is street parking in front."

If a caller asks about allergies, manager help, catering, or a complaint, send it to staff. That keeps the order moving without making the caller feel brushed off. ROAL is set up to do that handoff with a short summary, which is helpful when the dining room is full and the phone keeps ringing.

For menu questions, it helps to keep a short FAQ near the phone station. If you want a bigger list of common call types, see [menu, hours and allergen questions](/use-cases/menu-questions).

sections.h2: What if the caller wants delivery, pickup, or payment help?
sections.body:
Older regulars may be used to paying at pickup, or they may want delivery but dislike a complicated checkout. Keep the process simple and familiar. Tell them exactly what happens next and avoid extra steps.

Use this kind of wording:

"You can pay when you pick up. We do not take card numbers over the phone."

If the caller wants delivery, confirm the address slowly and repeat it back. If the caller is unsure about timing, give a realistic ready time instead of guessing. If the order is large, write it down carefully or let a phone host do it from the live menu.

Quick checklist for your staff:
- Confirm pickup or delivery
- Repeat the address back slowly
- Give a clear ready time
- Do not ask for card details over the phone
- Send special instructions to the kitchen

If you want a deeper breakdown of timing, fees, and address checks, see [phone orders for delivery](/blog/phone-delivery-orders-restaurant).

sections.h2: How should you set up the phone so older regulars can reach you easily?
sections.body:
If your phone rings a lot and the team cannot pick up right away, forwarding can help. That way, calls still get answered during rushes, breaks, or short-staffed shifts. The exact code depends on the carrier or system, so always confirm with your phone provider and test it with a real call.

Here are common examples:

| Phone setup | Common forwarding method |
|---|---|
| Landlines and some carriers | Dial *72 and the forwarding number to forward all calls; *73 to turn it off |
| AT&T, T-Mobile on many GSM mobiles | **21*number# for all calls; ##21# to turn off |
| Busy or unanswered calls on many GSM mobiles | **61*number# for unanswered calls; **67*number# for busy calls |
| Verizon Wireless | *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding |
| Business VoIP systems | Use the web portal |

A good setup for older regulars is simple: one main number, clear hours, and a backup path when the line is busy. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once you claim the host, and you can forward your existing number to it. That keeps your restaurant’s number in place while helping calls get answered.

sections.h2: What should you track so older phone orders stay smooth?
sections.body:
Do not try to track everything. Track the few things that show whether older callers are getting through and whether the order is clean. The goal is less stress at the counter and fewer corrections in the kitchen.

A simple weekly checklist:
- Were calls answered quickly?
- Were hours and address correct?
- Did the caller hear the ready time clearly?
- Did the kitchen get a clean ticket?
- Did any caller need help from staff?

Use your call history to spot patterns. For example, if callers often ask about parking, add that to your phone script. If they keep asking about one sold-out item, update the menu. If a regular caller always wants the same modifiers, make sure your team knows the routine.

takeaways: Older regulars often call because they want a simple, familiar ordering experience.
Slow speech, clear confirmations, and one question at a time reduce mistakes.
Use forwarding and backup call handling so busy shifts do not turn into missed orders.
ROAL can answer calls, take orders from the live menu, and send clean kitchen tickets.
Harder calls like allergy concerns, complaints, and manager requests should go to staff.

faq.q: How do I take phone orders from older customers without slowing down service?
faq.a: Use a short script, ask one question at a time, and repeat the order back once at the end. Keep the caller on a clear path: item, size, modifiers, name, phone, and ready time. If your team gets busy, an AI phone host can handle the routine calls and pass the harder ones to staff.

faq.q: What do older customers usually ask on the phone?
faq.a: They often ask about hours, address, parking, menu items, and whether a special or favorite item is still available. Some will also ask about delivery timing or payment at pickup. Keep answers short and concrete so they can write the details down or remember them easily.

faq.q: Should I let older customers pay over the phone?
faq.a: No, not if you can avoid it. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone, and payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes it. That keeps the call simpler and avoids extra risk.

faq.q: How can I make it easier for older regulars to order by phone when we are busy?
faq.a: Forward calls when needed, keep the menu current, and make sure someone or something answers with a calm greeting.
